In Danish, Jutland is Jylland, Zealand is Sjælland, Funen is Fyn, the North Sea is Nordsøen, and the Baltic Sea is Østersøen.

South of Zealand lie the islands of Lolland and Falster.

The North Sea is the largest of the seas around Denmark.

North of Zealand and Funen lies the water Kattegat, which in the south is connected to the Baltic Sea by the three straits Lillebælt, Storebælt and Øresund.
It is only in South Jutland, the southernmost part of Jutland, that there is a fixed land border, of 68 kilometres, to a neighbouring country, and that is to Germany.
The climate in Denmark is especially marked by the location by the North Sea and the short distance to the coast everywhere in the country.
From the Gulf of Mexico, a permanent stream of warm water, the so-called Gulf Stream, is carried towards Northern Europe.

Because of the Gulf Stream, the climate in north-western Europe, and particularly in winter, is markedly milder than the climate in other places in the world that lie just as far north, for example Moscow or southern Alaska.
The coldest months, January and February, have an average daytime temperature of three to four degrees, while the warmest, July and August, average about 22 degrees.
It can however become both considerably colder and warmer.
The lowest temperature ever measured in Denmark is minus 31.2, in 1982, while the highest is 36.4, in 1975.
Denmark is today connected by several bridges and tunnels.
In 1935, the first bridge over the Little Belt, Lillebælt, between Jutland and Funen was inaugurated, and in 1970 another Little Belt Bridge opened.

In the year 2000, with the Øresund Link, the Øresundsbroen, the Øresund Bridge, a fixed connection was created over the water of Øresund between Zealand and the neighbouring country Sweden.
Denmark's capital and largest city is Copenhagen, which lies on the eastern part of Zealand.

Aarhus, with about 300,000 inhabitants, is the largest city in Jutland.

A large number of Danish and foreign tourists choose each year to holiday in Denmark.
According to Denmark's national tourism organisation, VisitDenmark, 68 million overnight stays were registered in 2025 at hotels, hostels, holiday centres, campsites and in holiday homes in Denmark.

Many tourists also choose to see and experience a number of Denmark's sights, including the seven sites that are on UNESCO's World Heritage List.

This section is about some of Denmark's most important sights.
Skagens Gren is Denmark's northernmost point.
Here the two seas, Skagerrak and Kattegat, meet.
That means you can stand with one foot in each sea and see the waves clash together.
In 1795, the church south of the town had to be closed because it was buried by all the sand that blew in over it.
All that is left is the tower of "the Buried Church", Den tilsandede Kirke, as a monument to nature's enormous forces.

In the period of about 1875 to 1910, Skagen was in the summer an international meeting place for painters, kunstmalere, called the Skagen Painters, Skagensmalerne, such as Anna Ancher, Michael Ancher and P.S.
They searched for new motifs, and they found them in Skagen in the form of the fishermen and their hard life, as well as the special light reflected by the light beaches and the sea on both sides.
Most of the Skagen Painters' main works can be seen at Skagens Museum.
At Blåvand near Esbjerg in West Jutland, the Nazi occupying power began in 1944 to build Batterie Vogelnest, "Battery Bird's Nest", also called Tirpitz, with two enormous gun bunkers.
They were to be part of the gigantic defence work the Atlantic Wall, Atlantvolden, which the Germans wanted to build along the whole European Atlantic coast.
Denmark's location by the North Sea made the country a part of this defence work against a possible Allied invasion.
Therefore, from 1942, many bunkers were built and landmines laid along the whole of Jutland's west coast, Jyllands vestkyst.
The bunkers are not on Sjælland's east coast and not on Lolland's south coast.
Tirpitz was to have defended the approach to the west coast's only larger town, Esbjerg, with artillery that could shoot 55 kilometres.
But the bunker never managed to be finished before Denmark's liberation in May 1945.
After the war, Danish engineer troops tried without success to blow it away.
Therefore it and many other German bunkers still stand as a reminder of the occupation, in the west coast's magnificent dune landscape.
Tirpitz opened as a museum in 2017.
A tunnel connects the concrete in the new architecture with the old gun bunker with its more than three-metre-thick walls of reinforced concrete.
Parts of the Market Town Museum, Købstadsmuseet, in Aarhus, called Den Gamle By, "The Old Town", are a model of a small Danish town as it could have looked in the 1800s.
It consists of about 75 houses that have been rebuilt from all over Denmark.
The rebuilt houses are from the period 1550 to 1900, and the museum has continuously expanded with three new neighbourhoods with houses and shops from the most recent 100 years.
There are thus also parts of Den Gamle By that show how a Danish town looked from 1927 to 2014.
The spectacular museum building from 2014, designed by Henning Larsen's architecture studio in cooperation with Kristine Jensen's studio, lies a little south of Aarhus.
The museum's exhibitions contain especially finds from Denmark's prehistory, that is the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age, as well as from the Viking Age.
Among other things, you find Grauballe Man, who is the world's best preserved bog body.
About 290 before Christ, in the Iron Age, his throat was cut.
The reason the body is so well preserved is the chemical processes in the bog in East Jutland where he was laid.
When he was killed, he was 34 years old, and he was probably sacrificed to a god who was believed to live in the depths of the bog.
The Wadden Sea, which follows the coast from northern Holland across Germany and up to Blåvandshuk in south-western Jutland, is 500 kilometres long.
It is the world's largest continuous wadden sea landscape and one of the ten most important wetlands in the whole world.
Twice a day the tide pumps water in, so it becomes high tide, and out, so it becomes low tide, of the Wadden Sea.
This provides nourishment in the form of algae and plankton for an incredible amount of fish, mussels, worms and snails, which in turn is food for the larger animals in the food chain such as birds.
For example there can be up to 60,000 snails per square metre.
And the Wadden Sea therefore functions every spring and autumn as a giant restaurant for 10 to 12 million migratory birds.
Including several threatened species that stop here on their long journey from south to north in spring and north to south in autumn.
Among the biggest experiences at the Wadden Sea is the phenomenon "Black Sun", Sort Sol, when hundreds of thousands of starlings settle down for the night and perform a fascinating bird ballet.
The Wadden Sea Centre southwest of Ribe, designed by the Danish architect Dorte Mandrup, tells the story of the Wadden Sea.
Ribe arose as a market and trading place at the beginning of the 700s and is thereby the oldest town in Denmark.
Among the many traders from Europe were also missionaries who tried to convert the Danish population to Christianity.
In 855, about 100 years before Harald Blåtand as the first Danish king had himself baptised as a Christian, the German missionary Ansgar built a church in Ribe.
The town today has a particularly well-preserved town centre from the Middle Ages with cobbled streets and half-timbered houses.

Most central, however, is Ribe Cathedral, Ribe Domkirke, from the 1000s, 1100s and 1300s, which contains some very large, colourful modern glass mosaics and wall paintings with stories from the Bible.
They are made by the Danish artist Carl-Henning Pedersen in the period 1982 to 87.
Rold Skov is Denmark's second largest forest after Grib Skov in North Zealand.
Originally the forest consisted primarily of beech trees, but so many spruce and pine trees have been planted that today it is mostly coniferous forest.
Rebild Bakker, Rebild Hills, is a landscape with heath and stunted beech trees.
Part of the area was in 1912 bought by Danish-Americans.
Here you find the festival ground where every year a Danish-American celebration of the USA's Independence Day, the fourth of July, is held.
In Museum Rebild you can also learn about the more than 300,000 Danes who emigrated to the USA, especially in the years 1868 to 1914.
Rebild Bakker and Rold Skov are Northern Europe's largest area of natural springs of water.
The rainwater seeps down through the ground to the chalk of the subsoil.
Here the water is cleaned until it flows up to the surface again, when at some point it is pressed up again to the ground surface by the weight of the hills.
The chalk in the subsoil works like a sponge and stores the water, so it constantly has a temperature of seven to eight degrees, regardless of the season.
Among the many springs, Ravnkilde can be mentioned, whose pure water tastes wonderful.

Denmark's history is to a great extent marked by the country's location at the entrance to the Baltic Sea.
The shortest way into the Baltic Sea goes through the Øresund.
The town of Helsingør in North Zealand lies where Øresund is narrowest.
Therefore Helsingør has been decisive for being able to control the entry and exit of the Baltic Sea.
From 1429, ships that sailed through the Øresund had to dock and pay a tax, the so-called Sound Dues, øresundstold.
The dues became one of the most important incomes for the Danish king and the Danish state until it was abolished in 1857.
To secure the payment of dues, a castle was built called Krogen, which at the end of the 1500s was expanded into Kronborg, and rebuilt in the 1600s after a fire.
In Kronborg's underground fortress works, called the casemates, sits a statue of the legendary hero Holger Danske.
A well-known myth says that when Denmark is threatened by outside enemies, he will wake up to the country's defence.
Therefore one of the most important resistance groups during the German occupation of Denmark 1940 to 45 took the name Holger Danske.

Kronborg Castle is especially known abroad because it forms the setting of the English playwright William Shakespeare's play "The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark" from 1603, often shortened to Hamlet.
The play is about revenge, doubt and the relationship between life and death.
It is often quoted with the famous sentence "To be or not to be; that is the question".
The sentence is said by the living Prince Hamlet, the symbol of "to be", while he holds a skull, the symbol of death, "not to be", in his hand.
Roskilde Cathedral, Roskilde Domkirke, is regarded as Denmark's most significant church.
The construction began around 1200 and is the first larger brick building in Scandinavia.
Like many other cathedrals of the time in Europe, it is built in the so-called Gothic style, that is, it is marked by pointed, vertical arches that lead the eye upwards towards the sky.
Since the beginning of the 1400s, Roskilde Cathedral has been the Danish royal family's preferred burial church.
About 40 Danish kings and queens, more than anywhere else, are buried here.
Several tombs are placed in rooms that have continuously been built onto the church in the building style of the time.
A visit to the cathedral is thereby also an experience of many centuries of architectural history.
Queen Margrethe the Second's future tomb is in one of the church's side chapels, and here she will one day be buried next to her many predecessors on the Danish throne.
It happens in a sarcophagus designed by the artist Bjørn Nørgaard, who also made the tapestries for the Knights' Hall at Christiansborg.

The tombs of kings and queens in Roskilde Cathedral include King Christian the Fourth, born 1577, reigned 1588 to 1648, and Queen Anna Cathrine, 1577 to 1612, as well as King Frederik the Third, born 1609, reigned 1648 to 70, and Queen Sophie Amalie, 1628 to 85.
The up to 40-metre-high cliff in East Zealand facing the Baltic Sea is built up over millions of years of ancient layers of white-grey limestone, white chalk and flint.
In the middle of the cliff you see a black "line" in the form of a 5 to 20 centimetre layer of fish clay, which is about 65.5 million years old.
More clearly than anywhere else in the world, it tells about one of the biggest natural disasters in the Earth's history.
The ash layer is due to a meteor impact in Mexico, which spread death and destruction all over the world.
Perhaps this is also the reason that the dinosaurs and half of all the Earth's animal species were wiped out.
Højerup Church from the 1200s was built at a good distance from the cliff.
But still some of the church fell into the sea in 1928, because the waves over time have reduced the cliff.
Today the coast, and thereby the church, has been protected from more collapses.
Møns Klint lies, as the name says, on the island of Møn in the Baltic Sea.
The high chalk cliffs are under constant change, because the sea eats away at the cliff.
Dronningestolen, the Queen's Chair, at 128 metres, is the cliff's highest point.
Geocenter Møns Klint tells about the formation of the cliff 70 million years ago.
In the sea lived algae with a skeleton of lime.
When the algae died, the lime fell down on the seabed, where over millions of years a thick layer of chalk arose from the lime.
Afterwards the look of the globe changed a lot, as the landmass rose.
And in the ice age the ice caps pushed the chalk together into a giant mountain, which became Møns Klint.
The remains of some of the animals that lived in the sea 70 million years ago, you find today along the cliff beach as so-called fossils.
This applies especially to sea urchins, but you also find, for example, teeth from sharks, and there are also fossils of squid.
To get from the top of the cliff down to the beach you can use the Maglevandstrappen, which at 497 steps is Denmark's longest staircase.
In 2021 an entirely new museum opened about the poet and his beloved fairy tales in Odense's H.C.
It is designed by the Japanese architect Kengo Kuma, and the ambition has been to give visitors a many-sided artistic experience with sound, light and pictures.
Via a so-called biographical ramp you come down underground, where the fairy tales can be experienced.
The entrance to the museum is found right by the little yellow house from 1799, where the poet was probably born in 1805.
The castle Hammershus was built in the 1200s by the Archbishop of Lund in Skåne.
Until the 1500s it was the church that owned large parts of Bornholm.
Hammershus is placed on a lonely rock a good 70 metres above sea level and was thereby easy to defend.
In 1743 Hammershus was abandoned, when the invention of cannons and other new weapons made Hammershus less relevant.
It was afterwards used as a quarry.
That means the population in the local area used its building stones to build houses and other new buildings.
Today Hammershus is Northern Europe's largest castle ruin.
Bornholm is not least known for its four round churches, rundkirker.
Østerlars Church from about 1150 is the largest and perhaps also the oldest.
It was of course a church for local residents, but at the same time it is built as a refuge and defence work against enemies.
Those who defended the church were in the church's upper floors.
The narrow, round stairs and passages made it difficult for the enemies to get up there, at least more than one at a time.

The name Copenhagen, København, originally means "the Merchants' Harbour".
In the 1000s, the town was a fishing hamlet called Hafn, Harbour.
In 1167, Roskilde's bishop Absalon built a castle on the spot.
The town continued to belong to Roskilde's bishop until 1416, when it was taken over by the king.
That Copenhagen grew up as the country's biggest town has especially to do with its location by the Øresund, and thereby the big, international trade routes into and out of the Baltic Sea.
In addition the town lies in the lee of Amager and thereby has a naturally protected harbour.
The short distance, about 40 kilometres, to Kronborg in Helsingør also made Copenhagen an obvious bastion for the navy to support the guarding of ships' entry and exit through the strait.
In the Middle Ages, roughly 1050 to 1500, the king travelled most of the time around the country with his officials and soldiers.
But during the 1400s and 1500s, Copenhagen gradually became his permanent residence town and thereby the realm's undisputed capital.
It was not least during Christian the Fourth's reign, 1588 to 1648, that Copenhagen grew into a European city.
Christian the Fourth's buildings in Copenhagen.
The building-happy king put his mark on Copenhagen in the 1600s with a long series of striking buildings.
Perhaps the best known and most loved of his buildings is the Round Tower, Rundetårn, from 1642.
It is 41.55 metres high and famous for the 200-metre-long spiral walkway that leads up to the viewing platform.
Here you see the letters RFP, which stand for Christian the Fourth's motto, the Latin Regna firmat pietas, "Piety strengthens the realms".
Christian the Fourth bought, at the beginning of the 1600s, several private plots outside Copenhagen's then ramparts and created the King's Garden, Kongens Have.
Since the 1770s it has been open to everyone, and today it is one of Copenhagen's most popular parks.
In the garden he built a small summerhouse, which was continuously expanded and in 1634 was finished as Rosenborg Castle.
The crown jewels are found in the Treasury at Rosenborg and consist primarily of four large sets of jewellery.
The Queen normally wears them for the New Year's reception and at state visits and other big events.
In the Treasury you also see the so-called crown regalia, namely especially the orb and the sceptre, which symbolise the kings' or queens' power and dignity.
The king wanted to make Copenhagen a European trading centre, and therefore he built the Stock Exchange, Børsen, which was finished in 1640.
The Stock Exchange's characteristic is the Dragon Spire with the four dragon tails that twist around each other.
It is said to protect the house against enemy attacks and fire.
It did not protect any better, however, than that half of the building, including the Dragon Spire, was destroyed by a big fire in April 2024.
The unique neighbourhood Nyboder is also due to Christian the Fourth.
He decided in 1631 that good housing should be built for the navy's soldiers, and the district includes 200 terraced houses of about 40 square metres each.
In the 1700s Nyboder had 6,000 inhabitants; today a good 2,000 people with a connection to the Defence live here.
Amalienborg is the royal family's residence in Copenhagen.
The palace is named after Queen Sophie Amalie, who lived from 1628 to 85, and who was married to Frederik the Third.
The Queen had a palace built, which she named after herself: Sophie Amalienborg.
The present palace on the site, where the name is shortened to Amalienborg, has four almost identical mansions, which were built by rich noble families in the 1700s.
In fact it was not meant that the royal family should live at Amalienborg.
But when Christiansborg burned for the first time in 1794, it had nowhere to live and therefore bought Amalienborg.
It is from his reception room in one of the mansions that the king every New Year's Eve, nytårsaften, at 6 pm gives his New Year's speech to the whole realm community.

Amalienborg is where the king and family live; Rosenborg is a museum for the crown jewels.
On special days in the royal house there is a tradition for the king and family to be cheered from the mansion's balcony.
The Royal Life Guards with the big bearskin hats change guard at Amalienborg every day at 12 noon.
On special occasions, for example on the king's birthday, the Life Guards are in red uniforms.
Otherwise the guards are in blue.
When Tivoli opened in 1843, there was probably nobody who would have believed that an amusement park had been created that would become known in large parts of the world.
Denmark's most visited tourist attraction is known for its exotic architecture and historic buildings.

In the evening thousands of coloured lights create a fairy-tale atmosphere.
Finally there is the Pantomime Theatre, where the oldest of the theatre's pantomime performances are more than 200 years old.
The Little Mermaid, Den lille Havfrue.

Andersen's fairy tale from 1837 of the same name.

This sculpture from 1913, which sits on a stone in Copenhagen Harbour, is only 125 centimetres high, but it is one of Denmark's best known and most visited tourist attractions.
The Little Mermaid has several times been subjected to vandalism, for example by someone painting it with political messages or sawing its head or arms off.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Nine: Denmark and the Nordic countries.
Many Danes feel that they have particularly strong ties to their Nordic neighbouring countries.
That is because there are significant historical, cultural, political and linguistic similarities between the countries.
People therefore often speak about a kind of "family" of the five Nordic countries: Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland.
A very visible symbol of this community is that all five countries, with different colour combinations, have the same cross in their flag.
The four other Nordic countries have a somewhat different geography from Denmark, which makes up a small and relatively densely populated area.
Sweden, Norway, Finland and Iceland are all far bigger, but in return they are Europe's four most thinly populated countries.
These countries generally have a colder climate than Denmark and much larger areas with wild nature, and in several places, especially in Norway, also with mountains.
Sweden, with 10.7 million inhabitants, is the country in the Nordic region with the largest population.
Iceland, with under 400,000 inhabitants, has by far the smallest population, which is thus not much bigger than the population of Aarhus.
Both Norway and Finland, with 5.7 and 5.6 million respectively, have a population almost like Denmark's of 6 million.
The Nordic countries' history is to a great extent woven together.
The relationship has, however, not always been harmonious.
The Kalmar Union, 1397 to 1523, which is the only period where the whole of the Nordic region has been politically united, ended with Sweden breaking out after decades of hard fighting.
This was followed by a time, 1563 to 1721, with many big wars between Denmark-Norway on the one side and Sweden on the other about power over the Nordic region and the Baltic Sea.
In Denmark these wars are often called "the Swedish Wars", svenskekrigene.
A painting shows the Swedish siege of Copenhagen in 1658 to 60.
There are also chapters in history that the Nordic populations look back on together with a certain nostalgia.
The Viking Age and the old Nordic mythology, Asatro, are an important common feature in the history of Denmark, Sweden, Norway and Iceland.
At that time the common language, Old Norse, was also spoken, from which the present Danish, Swedish, Norwegian and Icelandic languages have all developed.
The four languages are thus closely related.
Since the Middle Ages, Danish, Swedish and Norwegian, unlike Icelandic, have taken in many words from other languages, first and foremost from German.
The three languages have kept and further developed so many common features that Danes, Swedes and Norwegians can relatively easily read and understand each other's languages.
The majority of the Finnish population has completely different roots from the population in the other Nordic countries, and the Finnish language is therefore very different.
But in Finland both Finnish and Swedish are official languages, and almost all pupils learn both languages in school.

This is because Finland was ruled from Sweden from the 1200s until 1809 and has therefore for a long time been considerably marked by Swedish language and culture, and in addition has a Swedish-speaking minority.

And in Iceland it is also, because of the country's long-lasting connection with Denmark, 1380 to 1944, when Iceland decided by a referendum, folkeafstemning, to become an independent republic, independent of Denmark, common to learn Danish in school as a foreign language.
Thus a certain linguistic connection of all five countries has been preserved.
The Nordic countries all became Christian and professed the Catholic faith in the Viking Age and the Middle Ages.
In connection with the Reformation in the 1500s, the Nordic churches broke with Catholicism and the Pope to instead become Protestant, evangelical Lutheran.
That has been the dominant denomination in the Nordic region to this day.

Since the Second World War, the Nordic countries have especially made themselves noticed by having succeeded both in becoming some of the richest countries in the world and at the same time being among the countries with the greatest economic equality.
People often speak of the Nordic welfare model.

It is characterised, among other things, by the state offering a long series of welfare benefits, for example education, health and elderly care, to all citizens, and by this welfare being paid for jointly by the whole population via taxes and duties.
The countries' foreign policy has had both differences and common features.
Their relationship to the EU and NATO has been different.
Norway and Iceland stand outside the EU, while Finland and Sweden only became members of NATO in 2023 and 2024 respectively.

Conversely all the Nordic countries are known for giving high priority to the UN and international peace work and are also among the countries in the world that give the most in development aid to the poor world.

Further, there is an official Nordic cooperation, which aims to strengthen the political, economic and cultural ties in the Nordic region, for example within environment, culture, research and defence.

They cooperate in the Nordic Council, Nordisk Råd, which consists of politicians from the national parliaments, and in the Nordic Council of Ministers, Nordisk Ministerråd, which consists of ministers from the countries' governments.
The members are Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Iceland and Finland as well as the self-governing areas Greenland and the Faroe Islands, under Denmark, and the Åland Islands, under Finland.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Ten: Danish science and thinking.
Research and innovation are today one of the basic preconditions of the Danish economy and thereby Danish welfare.
Danish research takes place to a large extent at the Danish universities, but research is also done at, for example, university hospitals, museums, libraries and archives.
In addition, a lot of research takes place in private business.
Especially within medicine, biochemistry and technology, Denmark is internationally known for its research.
Danish research at an international level has roots far back in time.
Several Danish scientists have over time helped shape international scientific development.
One of the first Danish scientists was the astronomer Tycho Brahe, who lived from 1546 to 1601, a nobleman from Skåne, who in 1559 came to Copenhagen to study at the university.
He was mathematically gifted, constructed astronomical instruments and made the until then most precise mapping of the starry sky.
One of Tycho Brahe's great achievements was to discover a new star, Nova Stella, in the constellation Cassiopeia.

Tycho Brahe's observations became important not least because the world-famous German astronomer Johannes Kepler, who lived from 1571 to 1630, used them to shape his groundbreaking laws about how the planets move around the sun.
Niels Steensen, who lived from 1638 to 86, also contributed to science in the 1600s.
Like Tycho Brahe, he did not accept the established explanations, but put emphasis on his own observations.
Niels Steensen was trained as a doctor and travelled to the Netherlands, where he made important discoveries within anatomy, that is the structure of the body.
Among other things, he was the first to show how we cry, and further that the heart is a muscle and not, as had until then often been believed, the home of the soul and feelings.

The astronomer and physicist Ole Rømer, who lived from 1644 to 1710, made an important scientific discovery when in 1676 he found out that light had "a hesitation", that is, that it does not spread immediately, but moves with a given speed from source to receiver.
Later he described new methods for measuring weight and distance.
He also did the preparatory work to get the present, Gregorian, calendar introduced in Denmark in the year 1700.
Until the beginning of the 1700s, it was not known whether Asia and North America were connected by land.
To explore this question, the Russian tsar, emperor, Peter the Great sent out in 1725 an expedition led by the Danish naval officer and explorer Vitus Bering, who lived from 1681 to 1741.
In 1728, Vitus Bering's expedition succeeded in sailing up through the strait that separates Siberia and Alaska, and thereby proved that Asia and North America are separated by water.
Some years later Vitus Bering returned as leader of a new and even bigger expedition that was to map Alaska's coast.
On the way home the expedition was stranded on a small deserted island off Russia's east coast, where it had to overwinter in extreme cold and without wood for heating.
Many died, including Vitus Bering himself.

He is buried on the island, which today bears his name, Bering Island, just as the sea it lies in is called the Bering Sea, and the strait that separates Siberia and Alaska is called the Bering Strait.
Ørsted, who lived from 1777 to 1851, discovered that electric current produces magnetism, the so-called electromagnetism.
A connection between electricity and magnetism had already been described by the Italian philosopher Romagnosi in 1802, but Ørsted's work was more profound and gained spread in scientific circles.
The discovery of electromagnetism laid the foundation for the technological use of electricity in society and production.
It was also his ambition to make natural science accessible and understandable to a larger part of the population.
Among other things, he made an effort to give scientific concepts and terms Danish words.
For example, he came up with the words ilt and brint instead of the foreign words oxygen and hydrogen.
Denmark has also made its mark internationally within philosophy.
That is first and foremost due to Søren Kierkegaard, who lived from 1813 to 55.
In his 42 years of life he managed to write a series of significant works within philosophy, theology, psychology and poetry.
Enten – Eller, "Either/Or", from 1843, is one of his most important works.
Søren Kierkegaard is regarded as the founder of existentialist philosophy, which assumes that every human being becomes who they are through the choices they make.

In the middle of the 1800s, ideas about women's liberation and equality between the sexes were formulated by the author Mathilde Fibiger, who lived from 1830 to 1872, who published the epistolary novel Clara Raphael.

Contrary to the ideals of the time about marriage, Mathilde Fibiger never married but was employed as a telegraphist at the Danish State Telegraph as Denmark's first female civil servant.

The Danish-Greenlandic polar explorer Knud Rasmussen, who lived from 1879 to 1933, has been of great importance for the exploration of Greenland and other Arctic areas.

On his seven expeditions in all, the so-called Thule Expeditions, 1912 to 33, he mapped the geography of the areas, collected thousands of objects, for example hunting tools, jewellery and furs, and an extensive knowledge about the Inuit, a number of Arctic peoples.

In the 20th century the Danish physicist Niels Bohr, who lived from 1885 to 1962, achieved international fame.
As a young man he set up a model of the structure of atoms.
For it he received in 1922 the Nobel Prize in Physics.
His most important scientific discovery was however within the so-called quantum mechanics, where Niels Bohr worked together with other leading international researchers.
Niels Bohr took an active part in the political debate about atomic energy and atomic weapons, which his research had made it possible to develop.
The seismologist and geophysicist Inge Lehmann, who lived from 1888 to 1993, proved in an article in 1936, through observations of earthquakes in New Zealand, that the Earth has an inner core.
She was successful as a researcher in the USA, and her studies were used by the American military to calculate the explosive force of test explosions of Soviet atomic bombs during the Cold War.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Eleven: church and religion in Denmark.
There is freedom of religion in Denmark.
It ensures that citizens have the right to unite in religious communities to practise their faith in the way they wish.
Freedom of religion was written into the constitution in 1849 as one of the fundamental freedoms of the new democracy.
Freedom of religion means that the individual citizen can practise the religion he or she wishes.
Everyone can also freely change religion.
You can also choose not to be a believer.
All citizens in Denmark have the same civil and political rights, regardless of whether they have one, another or no religious faith.
Denmark's monarch, the king, is as the only person not covered by freedom of religion.
The constitution establishes that the monarch must belong to the evangelical Lutheran, Protestant, church.
The evangelical Lutheran church is the Danish national church, folkekirken, and is supported by the state.
This is established in the constitution.
The state gives grants to the national church.
The members of the national church pay a special church tax.
The church tax is a kind of membership fee for the national church.
It is therefore only members of the national church who have to pay church tax.
The Danish national church and Christianity have left many traces in Danish society.
Everywhere in the country churches stand as clear symbols of the long history of Christianity in Denmark.
Christianity has helped influence the development of Danish society.
Church festivals and holy days are still marked during the year.
And the Danish national church carries out on behalf of the state a number of tasks, for example registering births, naming and deaths.
The church has done this for several hundred years.
It is one of the characteristics of the Danish national church that no one can speak on behalf of the church.
The national church has no official spokesperson.
Nor does it take part as a national church in the political debate.
Most Danes regard religion as a private matter.
There is a tradition for distinguishing between religion and politics.
The Danish national church is often highlighted as being a broad and roomy church.
That means it makes room for significant differences in the understanding of evangelical Lutheran Christianity.
The majority of the Danish population, about 70 percent in 2026, is a member of the national church.
There are, however, large geographical differences.
In Copenhagen Municipality, 46 percent of the population are members, while in thinly populated areas it is typically far more, for example 84 percent in Jammerbugt Municipality in North Jutland.
You do not have to be a member of the national church to be a Danish citizen.
Roughly seven out of ten are members, not one in three or one in two.
A member of the national church can thus freely leave if they wish.
It varies greatly how often members come to church for services or on other occasions.
The national church's organisation is, like all other public institutions, democratic and builds on the members' participation.
Since ancient times the word "sogn", parish, has been used as the name of the geographical area where the local church's members live.
A church parish is led by a parish council, menighedsråd.
It consists of the parish's priests as well as members who are elected democratically by the congregation.
The highest administrative authority in the national church is the Minister for Ecclesiastical Affairs, kirkeministeren.
Long before freedom of religion was introduced, the king had given special permission for Jews as well as Roman Catholic and Reformed Christians to practise their faith in Denmark.
Since the constitution was introduced, citizens have used freedom of religion to form many different congregations or religious communities.
Some build, like the national church, on the evangelical Lutheran understanding of Christianity.
They simply wish to stand freely and independently in relation to the national church.
Others build on some of the many other understandings of Christianity that exist around the world.
In addition there are also congregations or religious communities in Denmark within most of the other religions that are most widespread in the world.
A group of citizens can freely form a congregation or a religious community.
It does not need to be registered or recognised by any public authority.
It does say in the constitution, however, that it is a condition that "nothing is taught or done that is contrary to morality or public order".
This means that in religious worship too, you must respect the other rules that apply in society.
Religious communities or congregations can themselves employ religious preachers, that is priests, imams, rabbis and so on.
They can also build or furnish buildings to practise their religion, for example churches, temples, synagogues or mosques.
You just need, as with all other building, permission from the municipality.
It is to ensure that the building can take place within the framework laid down in local plans and so on.
Congregations or religious communities can also set up schools.
They can get permission to establish burial grounds.
And they can of course, like everyone else, use freedom of expression, for example to publish religious writings.

A religious community whose purpose is to gather around a faith in powers, for example a god, which stand above humans and the laws of nature, can apply to be recognised as a religious community or as a congregation.
Such recognition gives the possibility of a series of special rights.
In the religious area, this concerns especially that the congregation's priest, or other religious leader, can get permission to perform weddings.
In 2026 there are a total of 435 recognised religious communities and congregations in Denmark.
Besides Christian ones, they include Muslim, Jewish, Buddhist and Hindu ones.
Recognised religious communities and congregations do not get direct financial support from the state.
The tax rules do however give various possibilities for them to get indirect support.
The second largest religious denomination in Denmark today is Islam, which comprises a number of different religious communities.
It is only membership of the national church that the authorities register.
Therefore there are no official statistics on how many citizens belong to the various other religions, congregations or religious communities in Denmark.

In Denmark, a number of public holidays, days of observance and special customs are celebrated through the year.
On many of these days children have the day off from school and adults have the day off from work.
Denmark is, by the way, one of the only countries in the world that does not have an actual official national day.
Fastelavn is another word for carnival.
It is a spring festival that can be traced back to the ancient Roman Empire and Egypt.
Fastelavn in Denmark was originally the entrance to the fasting period within the Christian faith.
According to old custom, children dress up and hit a barrel.
In the old days there was a live cat in the barrel, and the one who breaks the barrel is still called the cat queen or cat king.
Today there is sweets and fruit in the barrel.
Fastelavn is seven weeks before Easter.
The Christian Easter marks that Jesus was crucified, died and rose from the dead.
In Denmark Easter is often used for family parties.
From old times there is a tradition of giving each other Easter eggs.
The egg is an old fertility symbol.
Today Easter eggs are often made of chocolate.
In addition there is a tradition of eating lamb, since the lamb symbolises Easter's message that Jesus was sacrificed as an innocent lamb for people's sins.
Easter falls every year in March or April.
The labour movement's international day of struggle is celebrated with parades, political speeches and events all over the country.
Both the trade union movement and the parties that stem from the trade union movement, the Social Democrats, SF and the Red-Green Alliance, are behind these events.
With the Christian Pentecost, people celebrate that the Holy Spirit, according to the Bible, has come to earth.
Pentecost was originally the end of seven weeks of joyful celebration after Easter.
At Pentecost some have the tradition of getting up early to see the sun "dance" and of having a Pentecost lunch, for example by bringing a picnic basket to the forest.
Pentecost falls every year in May or June, seven weeks after Easter.
The fifth of June is Constitution Day, when people meet and in speeches celebrate Denmark's democratic constitution, Danmarks Riges Grundlov.
Denmark got its first constitution in 1849.
On the evening of the 23rd of June, Sankthans is celebrated.
The background for celebrating Sankthans eve is a mix of pagan folk tradition and Christianity.
The festival marks midsummer, and according to old custom bonfires are burned.
The name Hans is an abbreviation of Johannes, and Sankthans is in a church context a marking of John the Baptist's birthday on the 24th of June.
At Christmas, Jesus's birth is celebrated.
Christmas Eve is the 24th of December, when families gather, eat together and give each other presents.
Most dance around the Christmas tree and sing Christmas hymns.
Many also go to church for the Christmas service.
Christmas thus has roots both in Christianity and in pagan folk tradition with a marking of the winter solstice, when the day length is shortest, and from there we move towards lighter times.

Here many families gather for Christmas lunch.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Thirteen: N.F.S.
Grundtvig, Danishness, folk high schools and church life.

The priest, hymn writer and social commentator Nikolai Frederik Severin Grundtvig, who lived from 1783 to 1872, became a central figure in the development of thinking, culture and association life in Denmark in the 1800s.
His thoughts have also had very great influence on present-day Danish self-understanding.

Grundtvig was a theologian and worked most of his life as a priest, but his extensive involvement in social life and thoughts about what it meant to be Danish came during the 1800s to play a decisive role in the development of the broad population's national awareness, that is, its shared understanding of what it means to be Danish.
In other words, what is today often called "danskhed", Danishness.

He lived in the time when Denmark, with the loss of Norway, in 1814, and of Schleswig and Holstein, in 1864, became a small state, but in return got a uniform population where practically everyone spoke Danish.
That created the basis for a country with high social cohesion and was decisive for Grundtvig's ideas.
Grundtvig had many thoughts about how the population, who until then had obeyed the king's decisions without resistance, could become competent and equal citizens.

Central in Grundtvig's way of thinking was the concept "folkelighed", which meant that he took his starting point in the people, ordinary people and not, as before, the elites, for example the lords of the manor, the academics or the wealthy middle class.
This was the basis for all his thinking.

Folkelighed became for him a positive concept, which was to be central in everything, among other things in laws, rules, institutions and behaviour, which should therefore take their starting point in the broad population's, especially the rural population's, culture, way of life and view of the world.
And through broadly based enlightenment and education everyone was to be made part of the great national community.
In this way the social groups that until then had understood themselves as quite separate could be brought together into one united people, a nation.
Grundtvig's ideas also became the basis for the folk high school movement, højskolebevægelsen.
The folk high school, folkehøjskolen, was, according to Grundtvig, to be different from the existing schools and universities.
Here the students were not to learn by heart or take exams.
The teaching was instead to be based on "the living word".
The students were to learn to be curious and discuss.
The population was to "learn for life" at the folk high schools, to be enlightened in a broad sense about subjects such as for example Danish history, poetry or natural science.
In that way they could become competent citizens with responsibility both for themselves and for the whole.
Important parts of folk high school life were lectures and community singing.
Since 1894 the Folk High School Songbook, Højskolesangbogen, has come out in many editions.
It contains numerous patriotic songs and hymns, which among others Grundtvig himself has written.

The folk high school was aimed especially at young men and women from the rural environment, in practice the children of farmers, bøndernes børn, not the children of the estate owners, godsejernes børn, and not workers' children.
They had, in Grundtvig's opinion, a particular need for teaching that could awaken the students' natural interest and zest for life and thereby develop them into active and engaged fellow citizens.
The first Grundtvigian folk high school was opened in 1844 in Rødding in South Jutland, and soon many more followed all over the country.
Here the young people from the countryside could, on a winter's stay, get inspiration for their future active life at home in the local community.
It was, among other things, this better education of the rural population through folk high school stays that led to the great success of the cooperative movement at the end of the 1800s.
The importance of the folk high school movement became smaller as industrialisation progressed.
During the 1900s agriculture gradually lost importance, the move from country to town gathered speed, and the traditional school system was expanded.
Today the folk high schools are aimed especially at young people from the towns, who after the upper secondary school leaving exam want to develop personally before beginning a higher education.
Several present-day folk high schools have gradually become specialised theme schools, where for example sport or music is practised at elite level.
This type of folk high school has thereby moved somewhat away from Grundtvig's original idea of the folk high school as the nerve of general popular enlightenment.
Grundtvig also had great influence on Danish church life.
He has thus lent his name to the Danish national church's dominant direction, Grundtvigianism, which builds on an undogmatic understanding of Christianity with a starting point in joy of life.
Grundtvig first formulated his view of Christianity in 1832 with an expression that was typical of him, namely: "Menneske først – kristen så", "Human first, Christian then".
It is also because of Grundtvig that the designation "folke-" is part of the name of many words such as Folketing, folkehøjskole, folkeskole, folkebibliotek and so on.

Grundtvig was also a member of the Constitutional Assembly, Den grundlovsgivende Rigsforsamling, which drew up Denmark's first democratic constitution, which came into force on the fifth of June 1849.
It was especially due to his effort here that the Danish church has never become a state church.
The modern Danish church is a national church, folkekirke, which is supported by the state, but otherwise carries out its functions according to rules which the church itself lays down.
This is entirely in line with Grundtvig's thoughts about folkelighed, which also underlie the way the Danish nation sees itself.
Besides his church and political work, Grundtvig was Denmark's most productive author of patriotic songs and hymns.
In the course of his long life he thus wrote more than 1,500, and many of them are still found in the Folk High School Songbook and in Den Danske Salmebog, the Danish Hymnbook.

At almost all Danish church weddings, "Det er så yndigt at følges ad", "It is so lovely to walk together", is sung, and every New Year shortly after midnight many drink champagne and eat kransekage to the tones of "Vær velkommen, Herrens år", "Welcome, year of the Lord", both written by Grundtvig.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Fourteen: school and education in Denmark.
The education system is part of the foundation under Danish society.
First and foremost because education gives citizens knowledge that has value in working life.
One of the most important reasons for a society's economic prosperity and the individual's income is connected with the acquisition of knowledge that can be used on the labour market.
The labour market in a rich country like Denmark therefore to a great extent makes demands on citizens for education and skill.
That applies in relation to basic knowledge such as being able to read and write Danish, do arithmetic, speak English or other foreign languages.
And it applies in relation to more specific knowledge, both practical and academic or theoretical, depending on which education is concerned.
In addition, education is important because it gives citizens common knowledge, identity and the possibility of understanding their everyday life and society.
The history of the Danish education system goes back to the Middle Ages.
In 1479 the University of Copenhagen opened as the country's first.
But oldest are the Latin schools, which arose around 1200 in connection with the cathedrals.
The designation Latin school was kept until 1903 for many of the schools that prepared young people for university.
After the Reformation in the 1500s, children were taught in Martin Luther's Small Catechism, a handbook of the Christian faith.
It was the local priest or sexton, the priest's helper, who taught.
The children often went to school only one or two days a week.
In the 1700s a number of schools were set up.
From the end of the century, teacher training colleges, seminarier, were formed, which had responsibility for educating teachers.
The foundation for the Danish folkeskole came with the school act of 1814, where the rules for teaching were made the same for the whole country.
There is no compulsory school attendance in Denmark, but instead ten years of compulsory education, undervisningspligt.
That means all children must receive teaching for ten years.
Parents can freely choose between the public folkeskole and private schools or teach their child themselves.
There is, however, the requirement that the pupil must reach the same academic level as in the folkeskole, if the child is taught at home or at a private school.
Even though there is no compulsory school attendance, almost 100 percent of Danish children go to school.
The folkeskole comprises a one-year kindergarten class, børnehaveklasse, often called the 0th class, and a nine-year basic course.
There is furthermore the possibility of an extra year in 10th class.
The folkeskole has, according to the Folkeskole Act, the following purposes.

One: the folkeskole must, in cooperation with the parents, give pupils knowledge and skills that prepare them for further education and give them a desire to learn more, make them familiar with Danish culture and history, give them an understanding of other countries and cultures, contribute to their understanding of humankind's interplay with nature and promote the individual pupil's all-round development.

Two: the folkeskole must develop working methods and create frameworks for experience, absorption and the joy of doing, so pupils develop insight and imagination and gain confidence in their own possibilities and a basis for taking a stand and acting.
Three: the folkeskole must prepare pupils for participation, shared responsibility, rights and duties in a society with freedom and democracy.
The school's work must therefore be marked by freedom of mind, equality and democracy.
All subjects are common to girls and boys, and pupils are normally taught class by class and together throughout the school course.
The school cooperates closely with the parents, and parents can get influence on their child's school by becoming a member of the school's board and by taking part in parent meetings at the school.

Pupils have the right to form a pupil council and to elect at least two members to the school's board, where they sit together with parent representatives, representatives of the school's staff and the school's management.
From the 0th class up to the 7th class, pupils do not get grades.
But from the folkeskole's 8th class, pupils get grades in a number of subjects at least two times a year.
The school can in some cases give pupils standpoint grades in the 6th and 7th class together with other feedback.
After the 8th and 9th class, pupils take exams in many subjects.
After the 10th class, pupils can also take exams in many subjects.
The exams can be both oral and written.
The grading scale used in Denmark is called the 7-point scale, the 7-trins-skalaen, because it has a total of seven grades, steps.
There are two grades, minus 3 and 00, for failed performances and five grades for passed performances: 02, 4, 7, 10 and 12.
The highest grade is thus 12, and the lowest grade is minus 3.
The 7-point scale is used everywhere in the Danish education system.
It is voluntary whether you want to continue your education after the ten years of compulsory education.
The labour market in Danish society does however increasingly make demands on citizens for education and skill.
Ten years of schooling is therefore not enough to get most jobs.
All citizens in Denmark have access to many different educations, and by far most educations are free for the individual citizen.
The majority of young people in Denmark continue after primary school with one of the many youth educations, ungdomsuddannelser.
A youth education can be aimed at the labour market or at further education.
A vocational education, erhvervsuddannelse, can for example be within trade, office or craft.
Within the social and health area you can become a pedagogue's assistant or a social and health care helper.

There are several different upper secondary educations that give access to higher educations, and which include, among others, the general upper secondary school, stx, the business upper secondary school, hhx, the technical upper secondary school, htx, and the higher preparatory examination, HF.
The higher educations vary in length according to what you study.
Higher educations can be short, 2 to 3 years, medium-length, 3 to 4 years, and long, 5 to 6 years.
With a short higher education you can for example become a laboratory technician, computer scientist or building technician.
On the medium-length higher educations you can for example become a pedagogue, journalist, teacher or nurse.
A long higher education can for example be a university education within natural science, health science, social science or humanities.
You must normally have an upper secondary education to be admitted to a long higher education.
If you have a vocational education, there is also the possibility of being admitted to short higher educations and some medium-length higher educations.
There are also many offers of so-called continuing and further education for adult citizens in Denmark.
People often speak of the possibility of lifelong education.
You can educate yourself if you want a new job, within another area than the one you were originally trained in.
Or if, for example, new machines have come to a workplace that require special competences.
Adults have the possibility of taking a vocational education or courses at the vocational schools.
Adults can also take the final exam in individual subjects at folkeskole level or HF at one of the many adult education centres, VUC.

There is furthermore the possibility of taking a supplementary continuing and further education at business academies, university colleges and universities, for example an academy, diploma or master's education, just as there are various educational offers for adults with reading or spelling problems.
More people educate themselves for longer.
In recent decades there has been a marked increase in how long the Danish population is in the education system.
Many more pupils and students have come at the academic educations and far fewer at the practical ones.
In 1982, 36 percent of an age cohort took an upper secondary education.
That has grown to 72 percent in 2023.
Conversely the share of an age cohort that takes a vocational education has fallen from 36 percent to 19 percent in the same period.
Many more also get a long higher education.
About 6,000 students completed a master's degree in 1990, while it was about 10,000 in 2002.
In 2025, about 29,000 students completed a master's degree.
There is broad agreement that it is overall positive that by far most continue their education beyond the compulsory folkeskole.
But the development has led to a number of other discussions about the education system's organisation.

For example, skilled manual labour is lacking, for example cooks, carpenters or electricians, and therefore there has been a discussion of whether too many choose the upper secondary school and too few the vocational schools.
Another challenge is that on some higher educations too many have difficulty finding work when the study is finished.
At the same time too few choose educations such as for example pedagogue and nurse, or technical and natural science subjects such as engineer or computer scientist.
Therefore various measures have been introduced that are to get more students to study the educations that the labour market has the greatest need for.

For example, in 2014 it was decided to introduce the so-called "unemployment-based dimensioning", which puts a ceiling on how many students can be admitted to the educations where there has over a period been high unemployment for newly graduated.
This applies especially to subjects within the humanities and parts of social science such as for example art history, anthropology, philosophy or musicology.
More practice in the folkeskole and the upper secondary school.
Not least as a result of the challenges with the lack of skilled manual labour, education policy in Denmark is undergoing some significant changes in these years.
This is seen both in the folkeskole and at the upper secondary schools.
With regard to the folkeskole, a majority in the Folketing agreed in 2024 that theory and training in practical work are to a greater extent to go hand in hand in the teaching of the folkeskole.
Specifically, all pupils in the larger classes are in future to go on five days of work placement at a workplace.
There is also established a possibility that pupils can go on so-called junior apprenticeship.
That means that pupils in the 8th and 9th class can choose to go to school three days a week, while the last two are spent working and training in a local company.
In addition there are to be more practical elective subjects for the oldest pupils, and understanding of technology is to be part of teaching throughout the folkeskole course.
In 2025 the reforms came to the upper secondary school, where from 2030 a new business- and profession-oriented upper secondary education, epx, is established.
At epx the pupils are to meet a combination of practical and academic teaching.
There must be close cooperation with local companies.
Therefore upper secondary schools which offer epx must have workshops and laboratories where pupils can get practical skills.
At the same time the admission requirements to the general upper secondary school are tightened, which is therefore presumed to get fewer pupils in future.
The reforms also mean that epx gradually replaces HF and the 10th class.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Fifteen: family and family life.
The family has undergone big changes in Denmark through the last hundred years.
Especially since the 1960s, families have been influenced by new cultural currents and forms of living together.

Where the family, the nuclear family, kernefamilien, earlier almost always consisted of a man and a woman who were married, and their children, there are today other family types: unmarried cohabiting couples with or without children, couples of the same sex who are married or live in registered partnerships, single parents with children and single people without children.
Marriage between a man and a woman is still the most common form of living together and made up 73 percent of all cohabiting couples in 2026.
But the share of persons who marry has fallen markedly through the years.
For example, 88 percent of all 30-year-old women in 1970 were married, whereas the share in 2026 was only 31 percent.
At the same time both men and women are older than before when they marry for the first time.
That does not however mean that they wait to form couples.
Since the 1970s it has been common, especially among younger people, that couples live together even though they are not married.
Couples who live together without being married, "paperless marriages", do however not automatically have the same legal and financial obligations to each other as married couples.
In Denmark the aim is that homosexuals have the same rights and duties as all other citizens.
It has however not always been so.
Until 1933, sexual relations between persons of the same sex could be punished with a fine or prison.
And only in 1981 was homosexuality removed from the Danish Health Authority's official list of mental illnesses.
But in 1989 Denmark became the first country in the world to give two persons of the same sex the right to enter into a registered partnership, which has largely the same legal effects as a marriage.
Persons of the same sex have since 2012 been able to marry, including to be married in the national church.
The Netherlands introduced in 2001 as the first country in the world this right.
Since 2010, two persons of the same sex have also had the possibility of adopting.
The rainbow flag is a symbol of diversity and equality for LGBT+ persons.
It has also become more common than before that adults live alone.
The number of single adults over 18 has risen sharply.
In 2024, 55 percent of all adults live as singles, that is, they are neither married nor live together with a partner.

The rising share of adults who live alone must be seen, among other things, in connection with it having become more common to get divorced, but it is also influenced by the rising number of elderly people, where one of the spouses has died.
Danish society rests on respect for the individual human being.
This means that men and women have the same rights in political and economic life and in family life with regard to the right to start a family, get divorced and so on.
Children also have rights, even though they are under the age of majority.
The age of majority in Denmark is 18 years.
For example, children under 13 years may not work outside the home.
Parents may not hit their children.
Children who are exposed to violence by their parents, or who are otherwise treated badly, can be forcibly removed by the authorities and placed in care with another family.
When children become 18 years old and thereby of age, they can freely choose how they want to live their lives and with whom.
This means, among other things, that they can enter into marriage.
A man and a woman who wish to marry can enter into marriage in Denmark under certain conditions.
Among other things, both must have legal residence in Denmark and have reached the age of 18.
Marriages in Denmark can only be entered into on a voluntary basis.
It is therefore punishable, strafbart, to try to force someone to enter into a marriage that they do not themselves want.
Forced marriage, tvangsægteskab, can lead to prison, fængsel.
A spouse, whether it is the woman or the man, who does not wish to continue the marriage, has the right to separation for six months and then the right to divorce, skilsmisse.

If they do not agree, a spouse has the right to divorce immediately when there are special circumstances, for example infidelity or violence.

Many children live in turns with both parents and get new parents, "papforældre", and siblings, if the parents marry or move in with a new partner.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Sixteen: discrimination, antisemitism, hate crimes and extremism.
Denmark is built on ideals of, among other things, freedom and democracy.
These ideals are laid down in Denmark's constitution, grundloven.
The constitution for example determines that you can say or write what you want, freedom of expression.
The constitution also determines that you can choose the religion you wish, freedom of religion.
The constitution also protects the right to form associations, freedom of association, and to assemble, for example for demonstrations, freedom of assembly.
But it is illegal to misuse the freedom for certain forms of discrimination, diskrimination.
There is discrimination if you treat people differently and worse because of their faith, political conviction, skin colour, sex, ethnicity, sexual orientation, age and so on.
People often say that "freedom must be used with responsibility".
In general, ideals of equality and democracy have high support in Denmark, but there are also examples of discrimination.
Studies indicate that almost half of all citizens with a non-Western immigrant background in Denmark have experienced being discriminated against in some way because of their ethnic origin.

Studies show that applicants with certain foreign names have a harder time getting a rented home or being invited to a job interview, even if they are just as qualified as the applicants with typically Danish names.
You also must not publicly say or write anything that degrades, ridicules or threatens others because of, for example, their race, skin colour, faith or sexual orientation.
Likewise it is illegal to use your freedom of expression to publicly call for a crime to be committed, for example by calling for violence against a particular group of people.
You must also not publicly express your clear support for a terror attack that has already been committed.
Many of these rules are made to protect religious, ethnic and sexual minorities against abuse from the state and against abuse from other citizens.
To protect minorities you can thus punish crimes particularly severely if they are committed because of the victim's ethnic origin, faith, sexual orientation or similar.
Such crimes are also called hate crimes, hadforbrydelser.
In the period 2022 to 24, the police in Denmark registered 2,108 cases of hate crimes.
1,022 of them, 48 percent, were because of the victims' race or ethnicity, 756, 36 percent, because of the victims' religion, and 435, 21 percent, because of the victims' sexual orientation.
The crimes are typically hateful statements, violence, vandalism or threats.
This corresponds to 702 hate crimes on average per year in the period, or about two cases every day.
The Jewish minority in Denmark is an example of a group that is particularly exposed to hate crimes.
In the period 2022 to 24, the police registered 430 hate crimes against Jews.
That is a high number considering that only a total of 6,000 to 8,000 Jews live in Denmark.
More than half of the hate crimes committed in Denmark because of the victim's religion, and more than every fifth of all hate crimes in Denmark, were committed against Jews.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Seventeen: equality between the sexes.
Equality between men and women is today one of the Danish society's basic values.
It has not always been so.
There are still challenges, but there has clearly been more equality between the two sexes in Denmark over the last 150 years.

That is not least due to the women's movement's fight for women to have the same rights as men and to change society's traditional view of gender roles, for example whether the man should decide over the woman, or whether women can have sexual relationships before marriage.
One thing is that men and women have to a large extent got equal rights and duties in our society.
Another thing is that men and women still do differently in a number of important areas.
One of the most important questions within equality has been the fight for equal pay.
In 1914, men who worked in industry or crafts earned on average 55 øre per working hour and women only 30 øre.
And female teachers had until 1919 to make do with two thirds of the male teachers' pay.
The pay differences between men and women have gradually become smaller over the last 100 years.
A milestone on the way was when the Folketing in 1976, after demands from the EF, now the EU, passed a law on equal pay for the same work.
But there is still a bit missing.
In 2022, women earned on average 12 percent less than men in hourly pay across the whole labour market.

Calculations that take account of women's and men's different levels of, for example, education, work experience, industry and job function typically show a difference in hourly pay of 4 to 7 percent.
That the difference has become smaller is due especially to men over recent decades having fallen behind women when it comes to education.
Both sexes are better educated than before, but the development has benefited women most.
In 1960 about five percent of women and 16 percent of men in an age cohort completed a higher education, that is above upper secondary level.
In 2023 it is about 64 percent of women and 45 percent of men.
So today more women than men complete a higher education, en videregående uddannelse; the answer in Danish is kvinder, women.
In addition there have come more female leaders, although they are still in the minority.
In 2025 the share of female leaders in the Danish labour market was 32 percent.
At the top management level, however, the share is smaller: among members of companies' boards women make up 19 percent and 16 percent of the chief executives.
There is however a markedly larger share of female leaders in the public sector compared with the private sector.
A large part of the pay difference that remains is due to there still being most male leaders, and to men and women working in different trades.
The difference in pay between the different occupational groups in the public sector was determined over 50 years ago.
That is, at a time when society still looked less equally on the two sexes than today.

Therefore some of the traditional "women's trades", for example pedagogues and social and health care assistants, are placed considerably lower than the typical "men's trades", for example police officers.
There is however disagreement about exactly how much is still missing before there is "equal pay for the same work".
That is because in practice it is difficult to assess when work is "the same", that is, exactly what value different occupational groups' and different employees' work creates.
A further important question about equality concerns maternity leave.
In 2002 the present legislation came with 52 weeks in total: four weeks before and 14 weeks after the birth to the mother and two weeks to the father in connection with the birth.
Of the remaining 32 weeks of parental leave, father and mother must each take at least nine weeks.
The other 14 weeks can then be freely distributed between the parents.
In practice, however, it is still the women who take by far the biggest part, on average about 80 percent, of the leave, while men take about 20 percent.
The difference means that women, because of their absence from the workplace, do not rise as much in pay as men do.
Conversely men have less time with their children.
Some of this difference will presumably correct itself in future.
In 2017, a new international movement spread via social media and the hashtag Me Too, the so-called Me Too movement.
The movement's target was sexual offences and harassment.
The occasion was a series of accusations from several women in the American film industry about abuse.
There were many of them, as it turned out.
The movement quickly spread to many countries, where women stepped forward publicly saying that they too had experienced similar things.

In Denmark the movement only really broke through in 2020, after the TV host Sofie Linde at a gala show with an award ceremony for comedians began, in August 2020, to talk about something completely different from comedians, namely sexism, sexisme, and her own experiences within the TV industry with sexual harassment and offences.
It became a spark that lit a big fire.
Because from there the development went fast.
There were many who had similar experiences, not least in the media industry, the film industry, the music industry, cultural life and in political life.
This meant that prominent politicians were forced to resign, and that well-known media personalities lost their jobs.
Sexual offences and harassment are also found in many other places, but it is less visible when it takes place in less high-profile industries.
It can for example be shop assistants, social and health care assistants or nurses.
When sexual offences are committed by leaders or people in superior positions, it is also about power, because the employees, for fear of their careers, may find it difficult to say no.
Among other things for this reason the trade union movement has also got a focus on sexual offences.
One of the results is that many workplaces are working to change the culture at the workplace, make it easier for employees to report the offenders and crack down harder on offences when they happen.
In 2021 a so-called consent-based legislation on rape came into force.
It aims to better protect persons against unwanted sex.
As the law was until then, it was rape if violence, threats of violence or other illegal coercion was used.
Or if intercourse was carried out even though the victim was unable to say no, for example was unconscious.
With the new law you can also be punished for rape if intercourse is carried out without both parties having given consent, even if for example neither violence nor threats have been used.
A consent does not mean that both parties must say "yes".
A consent to intercourse can be expressed both by words and by action.

This is Chapter Six, Episode Eighteen: health and the health service.
Health is one of the areas that voters think is most important of all.
The health service is also the area, only surpassed by transfer incomes, that the public sector spends most money on in Denmark.
In 2025 the health service made up 9.4 percent of Denmark's total economy, and the expenses have grown quickly in recent decades.

The reason for this increase is partly that there are more elderly people, but the increase is especially due to technology constantly giving more and better, but also more expensive, possibilities for treating diseases.
Some way into the 1800s, life expectancy in the population was only about 40 years, and a large part of the population died already as children.
Since then public health has improved significantly.
The Danish population now lives much longer.
Life expectancy is, in 2024 to 2025, 83.9 years for women and 80.3 years for men.
Another result of the improved health is that the population has become much taller.
The average height has since the middle of the 1800s grown from about 165 centimetres for men and 155 centimetres for women to 180 centimetres for men and 167 centimetres for women.
The improved health is due to a number of different factors, which really began in the 1800s.
First, much more food can be produced.
That means everyone has enough to eat and can thereby also better resist diseases.
Second, medical science has developed considerably: science knows much more about bacteria, viruses and other things that make us ill, and thus also about how diseases can be prevented and treated.
Third, hygiene has improved with, for example, underground sewers, running drinking water, toilets and healthier homes.
There is also greater general knowledge in the population about how important good hygiene is for avoiding diseases.
Fourth, a health service has been built up where all citizens have access to go to a doctor and to hospital.
Copenhagen's Municipal Hospital, Københavns Kommunehospital, built 1858 to 63, was one of Denmark's first "modern" hospitals.
In the last half of the 1800s and the beginning of the 1900s, over 100 hospitals were built in Denmark.

From 1893 the state gave grants to sick funds, sygekasser, which were insurance schemes in relation to illness: if you paid a fixed contribution to the sick fund, you could in return get your expenses covered when you were at, for example, a general practitioner.
The sick funds existed until 1973, when they were replaced by an entirely public system: the public health insurance, den offentlige sygesikring.
The social development that has made us much richer in a few generations has not only given us the means for better treatment and got rid of many of the diseases that come with malnutrition.
At the same time it has given us the means to eat much more, fatty and sugary, food, and to smoke tobacco and drink more alcohol.

This has led to a big growth in Denmark, as in many other countries, in the number of so-called lifestyle diseases, livsstilssygdomme, that is diseases you have an increased risk of getting because of the way you live.
It can for example be diseases such as cancer, cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and COPD.
The changed way of living is among other things also reflected in the share of citizens who are severely overweight having risen from 5 to 6 percent in 1987 to 19 percent in 2023.
Lifestyle diseases are also decisive for the fact that, even though the majority of the health service is free, there is still "social inequality in health".
Because the unhealthy way of living is to a great extent connected with a number of social conditions, not least level of education.
There are thus more people with short education who smoke, eat unhealthily or exercise little or not at all.
Conversely there are slightly more people with long education, especially among people over 65, who drink a lot of alcohol.
But overall people with short education have greater risk of getting a number of diseases and dying relatively early than people with long education.
Unskilled workers live, for example, on average five to seven years shorter than academics.
A number of laws have been passed that are to get more people to live healthier.

For example you must be 16 years old to buy beer in the shops, with an alcohol content of between 1.2 and 6 percent, and 18 years to buy cigarettes, strong beer, wine and strong spirits, with an alcohol content of 6.6 percent and above.
In nightlife zones you must also be 18 years old to buy alcohol after 10 pm.
